passages.original: Dicit enim civitatem nescio quam, non enim nomen recolo, locasse apud tres arlifices terna simulacra Musarum, quod in templo Apollinis donum poneret, ut quisquis artificum pulchriora furmasset, ab illo potissimum electa emeret. Itaque contigisse ut opera sua quoque illi artifices aeque pulchra explicarent, et placuisse civitati omnes novem, atque omnes esse emptas, ut in Apollinis templo dedicarentur; quibus postea dicit Hesiodum poetam imposuisse vocabula. Non ergo Jupiter novcm Musas genuit, sed tres fabri ternas creaverint. Tres autem non propterea ilia civitas locaverat, quia in somnis eas viderat, aut tot se cujusquam illorum oculis demonstraverant;
passages.english: For he says that some city or other (for I do not recall the name) contracted with three artists for three statues of the Muses each, which it would set up as an offering in the temple of Apollo, intending to buy above all from whichever of the artists had fashioned the more beautiful ones, choosing them from him. And so it happened that those artists all turned out their works equally beautiful, and all nine pleased the city, and all were bought, to be dedicated in the temple of Apollo; and he says that afterwards the poet Hesiod gave them names. So it was not Jupiter who begot nine Muses, but three craftsmen who created three each. And that city had not contracted for three for this reason, that it had seen them in dreams, or that they had shown themselves in that number to the eyes of any of those [citizens];
passages.notes: Scanning errors silently corrected: 'arlifices' as artifices, 'furmasset' as formasset, 'novcm' as novem, 'ilia' as illa. 'He' is Varro, named in the preceding context. In 'ut quisquis artificum pulchriora formasset, ab illo potissimum electa emeret' the subject of 'emeret' is the city.

passages.original: 28. Sed sive ita se habeat quod Varro retulit, sive non ita; nos tamen non propter superstitionem profanorum debemus musicam fugere, si quid inde utile ad intelligendas sanctas Scripturas rapere poluerimus; nec ad illorum theatricas nugas converti, si aliquid de citharis et de organis, quod ad spiritualia capienda valeat, disputemus.
passages.english: 28. But whether the matter is as Varro reported or not, we nevertheless ought not to shun music because of the superstition of the profane, if we can snatch from it anything useful for understanding the holy Scriptures; nor ought we to turn to their theatrical trifles if we discuss something about lyres and instruments that may help in grasping spiritual things.
passages.notes: 'poluerimus' is a scanning error for 'potuerimus' (we can/shall be able). 'organis' may mean musical instruments generally rather than specifically organs.

passages.original: qui dicere ausi sunt omnes Domini nostri Jesu Christi sententias, quas mirari et prædicare coguntur, de Platonis lihris cum didicisse, quoniam longe ante humanum adventum Domini Platonem fuisse, negari non potest ! Nonne memoratus episcopus, considerata !; i- storia gentium, cum reperisset Platonem Jeremiæ temporibus profectum fuissc in Ægyptum, ubi propheta ille tunc erat (a), probabilius esse ostendit quod Plato potius nostris Litteris per Jcremiam fuerit imbutus, ut illa posset docere vel scribcre quae jure laudantur? Ante Litteras enim gentis Hebræorum, in qua unius Ici cultus emicuit, ex qua secundum carnem venit Dominus noster, nec ipse quidem Pythagoras fuit, a cujus posteris Platonem theologiam didicisse isti asserunt.
passages.english: who have dared to say that all the sayings of our Lord Jesus Christ, which they are compelled to admire and proclaim, he learned from the books of Plato, since it cannot be denied that Plato lived long before the Lord's coming in human form! Did not the bishop I have mentioned, having examined the history of the nations and found that Plato had travelled to Egypt in the time of Jeremiah, where that prophet then was, show it to be more probable that Plato had rather been instructed in our Scriptures through Jeremiah, so that he was able to teach or write those things that are rightly praised? For not even Pythagoras himself, from whose successors these men assert that Plato learned theology, lived before the Scriptures of the Hebrew nation, in which the worship of the one God shone forth, and from which our Lord came according to the flesh.
passages.notes: Scanning errors silently corrected: 'cum' as eum, 'considerata !; i- storia' as considerata historia, 'Ici' as Dei, and others. The '(a)' is an editorial footnote mark and has been omitted. The bishop is Ambrose, named in the preceding context. Augustine elsewhere corrected this chronology of Plato and Jeremiah (Retractationes).

passages.original: 47. Dc genere temperato est apud Cyprianum virginitatis illa laudatio : Nunc nobis ad virgines sermo eat, quarum quo sublimior gloria est, major et cura. Flos eat ille ecclesiastici germinis, decus atque ornamentum gratiæ spiritualis, læta indoles laudis et honoris, opus integrum atque incorruptum, Dei imago respondens ad sanctimoniam Domini, illustrior portio gregis Christi. Gaudet per ipsas, atque in illis largiter floret Ecclesiæ matris gloriosa fecunditas : quantoque plus gloriosa1 virginitas numero suo addit, tanto plus gaudium niatris augescit.
passages.english: 47. Of the moderate style there is that praise of virginity in Cyprian: "Now let our discourse turn to virgins, whose care is the greater as their glory is the more sublime. They are the flower of the Church's growth, the beauty and adornment of spiritual grace, a joyful nature deserving praise and honour, a work whole and uncorrupted, the image of God answering to the holiness of the Lord, the more illustrious portion of Christ's flock. Through them the glorious fruitfulness of Mother Church rejoices, and in them it abundantly flowers; and the more glorious virginity adds to its number, the more the mother's joy increases."
passages.notes: 'Flos eat' read as 'Flos est' (scanning error). The stray '1' after 'gloriosa' is a footnote mark and has been omitted. The quotation is from Cyprian, De habitu virginum 3.
